result.summary: Ulysses lies sleepless planning vengeance until Minerva comforts him, while Penelope prays for death. Thunder and a miller-woman's prayer give him omens, and he wins the loyalty of Philoetius. At the suitors' feast Ctesippus throws a heifer's foot at Ulysses, Minerva unhinges the suitors, and Theoclymenus foretells their doom and leaves.

scenes.title: Ulysses' sleepless night
scenes.summary: Ulysses lies angry at the misbehaving maids and plans the slaughter. Minerva reassures him and sends him to sleep.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses fears failing to kill many suitors alone and being hunted by their avengers.

scenes.title: Penelope's prayer to Diana
scenes.summary: Penelope wakes weeping and begs Diana to kill her, recalling the daughters of Pandareus and a dream of Ulysses.
scenes.stakes: Penelope fears being forced to marry a worse man than Ulysses.

scenes.title: Signs from heaven
scenes.summary: Ulysses prays for omens; Jove thunders and a weary miller-woman prays for the suitors' last day.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses needs assurance that his vengeance will succeed.

place.name: Ulysses' house, court and mill room

scenes.title: Preparing the house; Philoetius
scenes.summary: Telemachus asks Euryclea about the stranger, the house is readied, Melanthius insults Ulysses, and Philoetius laments his master and pledges help after Ulysses swears he will return.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks exposure and abuse while testing his servants' loyalty.

scenes.title: The suitors' feast
scenes.summary: An omen halts the plot against Telemachus. At dinner Telemachus defends Ulysses, Ctesippus throws a foot at him, and Agelaus urges Penelope's remarriage.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus risks violence from the suitors; Ulysses keeps his disguise.

scenes.title: Theoclymenus' warning
scenes.summary: Minerva unhinges the suitors; Theoclymenus sees their doom, is mocked and leaves. Penelope listens as the fatal meal approaches.
scenes.stakes: The suitors face death for their crimes; Theoclymenus risks being thrown out.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses scolds his heart to endure, a famous line of self-restraint.
Theoclymenus' eerie vision of blood and ghosts foreshadows the slaughter.

analysis.text: Patience and restraint before vengeance: Ulysses masters his anger while omens and loyal servants confirm that justice is coming.
The passage shows the importance of omens, guest-right and loyal service in Homeric society.

legacy.text: Ulysses' address to his heart ("Heart, be still") is echoed by Plato in the Phaedo and became a classic image of self-control.

fun_facts.text: The 'Sardinian' grin of sentence 95 reflects a Greek word, sardonios, which gave English 'sardonic'.

language_notes.text: The cloister here means the covered colonnade or portico round the courtyard of the house, where guests and servants might sleep.
Refers to the Cyclops Polyphemus, who trapped Ulysses and his men in his cave and ate several of them; Ulysses escaped by cunning.
A paunch is a stomach, here an animal's stomach stuffed with blood and fat, like a sausage, and roasted over a fire.
Their avengers are the suitors' relatives, who would seek vengeance for the killings.
Oceanus is the great river encircling the world in Greek thought; being dropped into its mouths means vanishing to the edge of the world, the realm of the dead.
The Erinyes (Furies) were dread goddesses who punished wrongdoing, especially crimes against kin. The sisters become their servants, a fate Penelope treats as a vanishing from the world.
"Would fain" means would gladly. Penelope says she would go even beneath the earth, into death, if she could remain faithful to Ulysses alone.
"Methought" is archaic for "it seemed to me."
The "cloister" here is the covered colonnade or porch of the house, not a monastery.
Thunder from a clear sky was taken as a divine sign; the woman reads it as meaning something for someone, and she asks that it fall on the suitors.
"Cloister" here means the colonnaded porch or covered portico around the court, not a monastery.
"Shift for himself" means look after himself without help.
An "undressed" hide is raw, untanned leather, a rough bed suited to a beggar.
The boatmen are ferrymen who carry people across to the island from the mainland; they brought the animals over.
"Saluted him with his right hand" means greeted him by taking or clasping his right hand, a gesture of friendliness.
"Bred like ears of corn" means multiplied abundantly; "corn" in British usage means grain.
Birds on the left were ill omens; an eagle seizing a dove signals the suitors' own defeat by a stronger power, so Amphinomus abandons the plot.
"Inward meats" are the entrails, such as liver and heart, which were cooked first and shared at a sacrificial feast.
"Cloister" here means the colonnaded hall or porch of the house. The number 158 is a footnote marker from the edition.
A hecatomb was originally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; here it means a large public sacrifice to Apollo.
"Sardinian fashion" refers to the "sardonic" grin, a bitter, grim smile. The number 159 is a footnote marker.
"Gainsay" means to contradict or deny.
"Suffering" here means allowing or tolerating. The number 160 is a footnote marker.
"Set their wits wandering" means Minerva made them lose rational control; their laughter is a divinely induced madness, not real mirth.
"Meat" here means food generally, the dishes of the feast, which now appear bloody.
"Cloisters" are the covered colonnades around the courtyard of the house; "night of hell" refers to Erebus, the dark realm of the dead.
Piraeus here is a man, Telemachus' companion who hosts Theoclymenus, not the later Athenian port.
"Importunate" means persistently demanding; the suitor means the disguised Ulysses keeps pestering for food.
The Sicels were a people of Sicily; selling guests there as slaves was a way of getting rid of them for profit.

context_notes.text: The maids had been sleeping with the suitors; Ulysses later has the disloyal maids punished.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Ulysses' protector goddess, associated with wisdom and craft; she often visits him disguised.
Diana (the Greek Artemis) was the huntress goddess, whose arrows were thought to bring sudden, painless death to women.
Venus, Juno, Diana and Minerva each give the orphaned sisters a gift; Jove (the Greek Zeus) is said to know all fates, yet they are still lost.
Grinding grain by hand was heavy daily work done by household women servants; this woman is the weakest of twelve and is left to finish alone.
Euryclea is the old nurse who raised Ulysses and later Telemachus; she is a trusted household servant.
The feast day was a festival, so the suitors would arrive early; the household prepares the hall and the meat.
The Cephallenians were Ulysses' people, from Ithaca and nearby islands.
Swearing by Jove (the Greek Zeus), king of the gods, and by the hearth, the sacred centre of a home, made an oath binding.
Amphinomus is one of the suitors, and is portrayed as more decent than most of the others.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) protects Ulysses and wants the suitors' offences to grow so that their punishment seems just.
Ctesippus' "present" is a cruel joke: the bath-woman is a servant, and he casts the beggar as a servant's equal.
Theoclymenus is a seer who fled Argos after a killing and was brought to Ithaca by Telemachus; his prophetic gift lets him see what others cannot.
Penelope sits where she can overhear the hall, which keeps her aware of events as Ulysses' vengeance nears.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses' angry heart is compared to a bitch growling to protect her puppies, conveying fierce protective rage barely held back.
Ulysses addresses his own heart as if it were a person, steadying himself by recalling the Cyclops ordeal.
His restless turning is likened to a cook turning a sausage over a fire, a homely image of anxious scheming.
Minerva's questions chide Ulysses and assert her proven divine support, reassuring him through confident rebuke.
Penelope speaks directly to Diana, who is absent, and gives voice to her despair with a violent, wishful prayer for death.
Day's grief is set against night's forgetfulness, which sharpens how her dreams deny her any rest.
Ulysses hears her weeping and wonders whether she knows him, while the reader knows she dreamed of him but has not recognised him.
Jove's thunder answers the prayer at once and hints that the suitors' doom is near.
The overworked servant's bitter wish for the suitors' last dinner shows how heavily they burden the household and makes her an unwitting voice of divine justice.
Ulysses' silent brooding shows his self-restraint as he endures insult while plotting vengeance.
Philoetius turns from the stranger to address Jove directly, voicing bitter complaint at the god's cruelty to mortals.
Philoetius weeps at the resemblance to Ulysses without knowing he is speaking to him in rags.
The disguised Ulysses' oath hints that his return and the killing of the suitors are imminent.
The eagle and dove prefigure the suitors' coming destruction at the hands of Ulysses and hint that the plot against Telemachus will fail.
Ctesippus pretends generosity while throwing an insult, and the beggar he targets is actually the master of the house.
Telemachus' threat shows how far he has grown from the passive youth of the early books into a man who asserts authority.
Telemachus swears by his father's sorrows while that father sits in the room in disguise, listening.
The vision of blood-dripping walls and ghosts heading to the underworld previews the coming slaughter of the suitors.
The suitors laugh at the prophecy while the audience knows it is true, making their mirth grimly ironic.
Theoclymenus answers Eurymachus' jibe about darkness by claiming his own sight and wits, implying the suitors are the blind ones.
The narrator openly comments on the coming meal and blames the suitors for their own doom, heightening suspense.
